newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Socialists to take up parliament seats.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Socialists to take up parliament seats.

text.p: Albania's Socialist party voted on Wednesday to take up seats in parliament boycotted since a disputed 1996 election won by the right wing, saying it would help a peaceful solution to the country's lawlessness.

Leaders of the Socialist Party, which includes Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, voted for the party's nine deputies to take up their seats in the 140-member parliament where President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party has 122 seats.

The group "will have political power and it is politics which counts today in Albania. If politics did not work we would be in civil war," Namik Dokle, a senior party member, told Reuters. The party voted 66 to nine to take up the seats.

Berisha, who has promised new elections in June in a bid to bring Albania back from the brink of near-anarchy, was forced to appoint Fino as head of an all-party government of national reconciliation on March 11 amid an insurrection.

He has repeatedly urged the Socialists, the former communists and main opposition, to take up the seats they won despite their boycott of the June 1996 elections. The Socialists allege the vote was rigged by Berisha's allies.

Western governments criticised the election as unfair following a report by election monitors of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, who said the poll failed to meet international standards.
"When we speak of holding free, fair and equal elections by June 1977 we have to do it with the complete legal context," Dokle said.
Albania descended towards chaos last month when protests at the collapse of fraudulent savings schemes spilled over into armed unrest. Scores of people have died and looting and banditry are rife.
Apart from bolstering the Socialists' democratic image, Dokle said the return to parliament would give the Socialists a greater voice in pushing for electoral reforms.
The Socialists especially want to scrap a "genocide" law which bans anyone who had a senior position in the former Stalinist regime that collapsed in 1990.
Leading Socialist politician Fatos Nano, an ex-prime minister freed from jail last month, is among those barred from running for parliament. "The law...denies a constitutional right," Dokle said.
He said other priorities included creating an impartial police force and bolstering media freedom.
But a minimum of 20 votes is needed to propose legislation, meaning the Socialists will be powerless unless they can win support from factions within Berisha's Democratic party.
